lessonTitle: Community Diagnosis: Needs Assessment, Primary Health Care and Social Determinants

blocks.text: Two neighbourhoods sit either side of one main road in the same city. Residents of one live noticeably longer than residents of the other, and the practices on either side see very different patients, even though they use the same guidelines. Treating individuals one at a time will never explain why. A community diagnosis asks what is happening to the health of a whole population, and why.

blocks.markdown: **What is community diagnosis?** Just as a clinical diagnosis summarises one patient's problem, a *community diagnosis* describes the health status of a defined population, the factors that shape it, the resources available, and the priorities for action. It is the first stage of the cycle that also includes planning, implementing and evaluating a health programme. The practical tool is the *health needs assessment* (HNA).

blocks.title: Health needs assessment
blocks.text: A health needs assessment is a systematic method for reviewing the health issues facing a defined population, leading to agreed priorities and resource allocation that will improve health and reduce inequalities. It combines epidemiological data (who is affected and how much), the views of the community, and an analysis of the services and resources already available.

blocks.markdown: **Steps of a needs assessment.** The first step is to define the *population* (geographical, practice list, or a group such as older adults) and the *purpose* of the assessment. You then collect data from several sources: routine data (births, deaths, hospital activity, practice registers), surveys, and qualitative methods such as focus groups and interviews with residents. The data are analysed and compared with other areas, then discussed with the community and stakeholders to set priorities. An action plan is agreed, delivered and its effects are evaluated, which feeds the next cycle.

rows: Normative
Need defined by experts or by standards
An expert guideline says all adults with hypertension should have regular review; some do not
Felt
What people say they want or feel they need
Residents tell a survey they would like evening clinic appointments
Expressed
Felt need turned into action (demand)
A long waiting list for a service
Comparative
Gap shown by comparing similar populations
A ward has a lower vaccination uptake than similar neighbouring wards
blocks.caption: Bradshaw's taxonomy of need is widely used to structure what data to collect; the categories overlap in practice.

blocks.markdown: **Measuring disease burden.** Two basic measures are *prevalence* (how many people have the condition now) and *incidence* (how many new cases arise over a period). Prevalence guides service planning; incidence reveals trends and risk. Both need a clear denominator.

blocks.latex: \text{prevalence} = \dfrac{\text{number with the condition}}{\text{number in the population examined}} \times 100\%
blocks.caption: Point prevalence from a survey.

blocks.title: Estimating prevalence from a community survey
blocks.prompt: In a community blood pressure survey, 1,060 adults were screened. Of these, 212 had hypertension according to the survey definition. Estimate the point prevalence.

steps.text: Identify the numerator and the denominator: 212 with the condition, 1,060 screened.
Compute the ratio and convert to a percentage.

Interpret: one in five screened adults has hypertension. However, the sample may not represent the whole community (for example, people who attend a screening event may differ), so describe how the sample was selected before generalising.
Compare with regional and national figures and decide, with the community, whether this is a local priority.

blocks.answer: Point prevalence of 20% in the sample; interpret with caution about representativeness.

blocks.title: Estimating an incidence rate
blocks.prompt: A health centre follows a stable population and records 30 new cases of a condition over a year in a population contributing 6,000 person-years. Calculate the incidence rate per 1000 person-years.

steps.text: State clearly the unit and the time period: 5 new cases per 1000 person-years.
Explain how it would be used: tracked over successive years, a rising rate would trigger investigation of causes and consideration of preventive action.

blocks.markdown: **Organisation of primary health care.** The 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration, reaffirmed in the 2018 Astana Declaration, describes primary health care as first-contact, comprehensive, continuing, community-based care that is accessible and affordable. Health systems are often organised in tiers: *primary* (first contact, prevention, long-term conditions), *secondary* (specialist and hospital services, usually accessed by referral) and *tertiary* (highly specialised services). In many systems, including the UK, the primary care clinician acts as a *gatekeeper* (also called a coordinator of care): patients access most specialist services through a referral, which protects specialist capacity and keeps care continuous. A good referral contains clear clinical information and a clear question, and the specialist returns information and advice to primary care. Community health workers and nurses extend the reach of primary care, particularly where doctors are scarce.

rows: Primary
Prevention, health promotion, first-contact care, long-term condition management, community nursing
Usually direct, self-referral or registered practice
Secondary
Specialist outpatient and inpatient services, emergency care
Usually by referral from primary care, or emergency pathway
Tertiary
Highly specialised services (for example transplant or specialist cancer services)
Referral from secondary care or specialised commissioning route
blocks.caption: Terminology and pathways differ between countries; the pattern of tiers is the point.

blocks.markdown: **Social determinants.** Health is shaped by the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live and age. The Dahlgren-Whitehead model places individual factors (age, sex, genetics) at the centre, surrounded by lifestyle behaviours, social and community networks, living and working conditions (housing, employment, education, healthcare, sanitation, food) and, outermost, general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions. Because the outer layers shape the inner ones, interventions aimed only at behaviour often fail to reduce inequalities; the Marmot reviews emphasise action across the life course on income, education, employment and housing. A community diagnosis should therefore describe these determinants and identify which can be influenced locally.

blocks.title: Needs assessment ends in action
blocks.text: A needs assessment that does not lead to prioritised, resourced and evaluated action has not achieved its purpose. Priorities are set by considering the size of the problem, its severity, whether effective interventions exist, equity, cost and community acceptability, and they must be agreed with the community.

points: Community diagnosis describes the health of a defined population and underpins health programmes; the health needs assessment is the practical tool.
Use several data sources (routine data, surveys, qualitative methods) and Bradshaw's categories of need; calculate prevalence and incidence with clear denominators.
Primary health care is first-contact, comprehensive and continuing; tiered systems use referral and gatekeeping to match patients to the right level.
Social determinants (income, housing, education, employment, environment) shape health and inequalities, and action must address them as well as behaviour.

questions.stem: A primary care network wants to carry out a health needs assessment for a new housing development. What is the appropriate first step?

options.text: Wait for hospital admission data to accumulate for several years
Define the population to be assessed and the purpose of the assessment
Commission a new clinic building immediately

questions.correctOptionText: Define the population to be assessed and the purpose of the assessment

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: an intervention before assessment may not target real needs.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: waiting delays action and uses only one data source.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: defining the population and the purpose is the first step.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: services should be planned after needs are understood.

questions.explanation: A needs assessment needs a defined population and a clear purpose before data are collected, otherwise the data collected will not answer the right question. Services and campaigns follow from the analysis, not before it.

questions.stem: In a community survey, many residents say they would like an evening clinic, but few of them have yet asked for appointments outside normal hours. According to Bradshaw's taxonomy, what kind of need is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is what people say they want, without it yet being turned into action.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: normative need is defined by experts or standards.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: comparative need arises from comparison with similar populations.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: expressed need is felt need turned into demand, such as a waiting list.

questions.explanation: Felt need is the need people perceive and report, whereas expressed need is demand, evidenced by people actually seeking the service. The survey records wishes but not demand, so it measures felt need.

questions.stem: Why do many health systems use referral from primary care to specialist care, rather than allowing unrestricted direct access?

options.text: It guarantees that patients never need a hospital admission
It eliminates the need for communication between clinicians
It is intended solely to reduce costs, with no clinical benefit
It matches patients to the appropriate level of care, protects scarce specialist capacity and supports continuity through a coordinating clinician

questions.correctOptionText: It matches patients to the appropriate level of care, protects scarce specialist capacity and supports continuity through a coordinating clinician

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: referral does not prevent admission.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: referral depends on good communication, with information passing in both directions.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: cost is a consideration but there are also clinical benefits, such as coordination and avoiding unnecessary investigation.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: gatekeeping and referral coordinate care and use specialist resources appropriately.

questions.explanation: Referral systems exist to put patients in the right place at the right time, with primary care coordinating continuing care. Good referral letters and feedback from the specialist keep the patient's care coordinated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a wider social determinant of health rather than an individual lifestyle behaviour?

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: inactivity is a lifestyle behaviour.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: housing conditions are part of living and working conditions.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: smoking is an individual behaviour, although shaped by social context.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: alcohol consumption is a lifestyle behaviour.

questions.explanation: In the Dahlgren-Whitehead model, housing quality is a living-condition determinant, which lies in a wider layer than individual lifestyle choices. These wider determinants influence behaviours and outcomes, so they are targets for community-level action.

questions.stem: In a tiered health system, secondary care is usually the first point of contact for most patients with common problems.
questions.explanation: Primary care is the first point of contact and handles most common problems, including prevention and long-term conditions. Secondary care normally receives patients by referral or through emergency pathways.

questions.stem: A community survey of 1,250 adults finds that 175 are current smokers. Calculate the point prevalence of smoking in the sample as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Prevalence is the number with the characteristic divided by the number examined: 175/1250 = 0.14. Multiplied by 100, this is 14%. The estimate describes the sample and generalises only if the sample represents the community.

questions.stem: A practice follows 12,000 person-years of observation of adults and records 36 new cases of type 2 diabetes. Calculate the incidence rate per 1000 person-years.
questions.explanation: Incidence rate is new cases divided by person-years at risk: 36/12000 = 0.003 per person-year. Multiplying by 1000 gives 3.0 per 1000 person-years, which allows comparison between populations of different size.

questions.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to carry out a community health needs assessment for an area with a high proportion of older residents.
markingGuide: Define the population (area, age group) and the purpose of the assessment
Collect epidemiological data: demography, mortality, morbidity, hospital activity, practice registers
Collect community views through surveys, focus groups or interviews (felt need)
Describe existing services and resources and compare with similar areas
Analyse for gaps and priorities, including inequalities; consider size, severity, effective interventions and acceptability
Agree priorities with the community and stakeholders and set an action plan
Implement and evaluate, then repeat the cycle
questions.explanation: A complete answer follows the cycle of define, collect (including community voice), analyse and prioritise, act and evaluate. Using more than one data source and involving residents are the hallmarks of a good needs assessment.

questions.stem: Describe how primary health care is organised, including the role of referral between levels of care, and discuss two problems that may arise at the interface between primary and secondary care.
markingGuide: Primary care: first contact, comprehensive, continuing, community based, includes prevention and long-term condition management
Secondary and tertiary care: specialist care usually by referral; emergency access separately
Gatekeeping or coordination by primary care clinician protects capacity and supports continuity
A good referral gives clear information and a clear question; the specialist feeds back information
Role of multidisciplinary team and community health workers
Problems at the interface: delayed or incomplete communication, inappropriate or unnecessary referrals, long waiting times, fragmented care, patient confusion over responsibility
Possible solutions: shared records, referral guidelines, advice-and-guidance, integrated care
questions.explanation: A good answer explains the tiers and why referral and coordination exist, then recognises that the interface is where information is lost. Solutions should be practical, such as shared records or clear referral criteria.

questions.stem: A community has high rates of childhood asthma and many families live in damp, rented housing on low incomes. Using the idea of social determinants, explain how these factors may be linked to the health problem and suggest two interventions at different levels.
markingGuide: Social determinants: housing quality (damp and mould as triggers), income and rental insecurity, education, access to services
Dahlgren-Whitehead model: wider determinants influence behaviours and outcomes
Individual or family level: asthma review, inhaler technique, self-management plans, smoking cessation support
Community level: working with housing providers and local authority on housing conditions, social prescribing, advice on benefits
Policy level: housing standards and income support (upstream action)
Evaluation and inclusion of community voice
questions.explanation: The answer should show that behaviour change and clinical care alone will not resolve problems driven by housing and income. Action across levels, from individual care to community and policy change, is the most effective.
